4	---
5	
6	# Brainstorming Ideas Into Designs
7	
8	Help turn ideas into fully formed designs and specs through natural collaborative dialogue.
9	
10	Start by classifying how much process the request needs, then work
11	through your path: understand the context, refine the idea, present a
12	design, and get your human partner's approval.
13	
14	<HARD-GATE>
15	Do NOT invoke any implementation skill, write any code, scaffold any
16	project, or take any implementation action until you have told your
17	human partner what you intend and they have approved it. This applies
18	to EVERY task on EVERY path below — the ceremony scales with the task;
19	the approval gate never does.
20	</HARD-GATE>
21	
22	**REQUIRED SUB-SKILL:** Use hyperpowers:communication for everything your human partner reads on every path: the questions, the approach comparison, the design presentation, and the spec.
23	
24	**After every context compaction:** Claude Code re-attaches this skill cut to its first 20,000 characters, which ends before the spec-writing steps, and a full Read you made before the compaction does not survive it. After each compaction, the first and every later one, Read this file in full before your next action (a question to your human partner, a visual-companion step, or writing the spec), along with any other skill you are following whose re-attached copy is cut short.
25	
26	## Three Paths
27	
28	Before your first question, classify the request and say the
29	classification out loud — "this looks bounded, so I'll present a short
30	design here rather than write a spec" — so your human partner can
31	override it:
32	
33	- **Spike** — a feasibility question ("can we...", "is it possible...",
34	  "quick and dirty is fine") whose output is an answer, not code you
35	  keep. Present the question and what you'll try in 2-3 sentences, get
36	  a nod, then find out as cheaply as correctness allows. No design
37	  doc, no spec file. Report findings as a recommendation; anything you
38	  built stays labeled throwaway.
39	- **Bounded** — a well-scoped change to code that already exists in
40	  this repo: a new flag, a small endpoint, a one-file fix.
41	  Understanding the kind of app is not enough — bounded means the flow
42	  you are changing is already here to read. If there is no existing
43	  flow to change, the task is not bounded. Classify by the outcome the
44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.
139

196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340

steps.message:
This is a bounded change, so I'll keep the design short and put it here in chat rather than writing a spec. The page, its script and its data are already in the repo, and filtering 311 events in the browser fits the settled API decisions in NOTES.md.

The first open question is where the filters go, and that's easier to see than to describe. I've opened a browser tab with three layouts at http://localhost:59961/?key=ec5b0f8e021ed66dd55946e7b37cb65a3a2ef65b3f5806ce7108f38cddc226f8. The tab uses a lot of tokens, so tell me if you'd rather stay in the terminal.

All three layouts have the same controls: event type, a "Failed sign-ins only" shortcut, and a result count. They differ only in placement:

- **A. Filter bar above the table.** I recommend this one. The controls are always visible, and the failed sign-in shortcut stays in plain view, which matters because every support ticket so far was someone looking for a failed sign-in. On a narrow screen the controls stack.
- **B. Side panel beside the table.** It takes width away from a table that already has six columns, so the table gets cramped well before you reach 320px.
- **C. A "Filter" button that opens a popover, with active filters shown as tags.** It's the most compact, but the failed sign-in shortcut sits behind a click.

The mockups are rough sketches. The real version will use the guideline components and tokens.

steps.message:
Here's the design for your yes.

**What it does.** A filter bar sits between the intro and the table, with:
- An event type select: "All events" plus the nine types.
- A "Failed sign-ins only" checkbox.
- A date range: "From" and "To" date pickers, with a presets select beside them offering Any time, Last 24 hours, Last 7 days and Last 30 days.

The table updates as soon as any control changes. Nothing submits and the page doesn't navigate. All the filters combine, so if you tick "Failed sign-ins only" while the type is set to "Sign-in", you get zero rows rather than one control quietly overriding the other. Above the table, a live region reads "Showing 4 of 14 events", and screen readers announce it without moving focus. When nothing matches, the table body shows "No events match these filters" with a "Clear filters" button.

Dates are picked and compared in the viewer's local time zone. The stored UTC values aren't touched.

The filter bar starts hidden and the script reveals it, so with JavaScript off nobody sees controls that can't work. The empty table without JavaScript is unchanged and goes into the follow-ups in NOTES.md, as agreed.

**Files**
- `public/tokens.css` (new): only the tokens the filter bar uses, with values copied from `01-foundations.md`.
- `public/activity.html`: links `tokens.css` and adds the filter bar markup, using a fieldset, visible labels above each control, and the live region.
- `public/activity.css`: filter bar styles, using tokens only. The existing raw values stay untouched.
- `public/activity.js`: the filtering, the count and the clear button. Rows are still built from `activity-data.js`.
- `NOTES.md`: adds the no-JS follow-up.

The estimate is about 200 lines, under the 300 limit. That makes two commits: `feat: add filters to account activity page` and `docs: note no-JS gap on activity page`. I'll show you the full diff before each commit and won't push.

**How I'll check it**
- Go through the token tables and component specs line by line against what I wrote: no raw hex values, no hard-coded px sizes.
- Open the page in Chrome and click through each filter, the combinations, a preset, a custom date range, the empty result and "Clear filters".
- Tab through every control to check focus rings, and confirm there's no horizontal scroll at 320px wide.

I'll report exactly what I clicked. If I can't drive a real browser from here, I'll tell you and ask you to do the click-through instead of claiming it works.

There's one spec detail I'll follow unless you say otherwise. The Select spec calls for a "Select…" placeholder, but here the event type select defaults to "All events", because a filter needs a real default state.

Does this design work for you? I'll start once you say yes.
Yes, that works. Go ahead.

Each semantic token resolves to a palette token per theme. The dark theme is

| `--danger-fill-hover` | `red-700` | `red-400` | Destructive button hover |

One scale, used for padding, gaps, and margins alike. Steps are named by index,

# 03 Forms

How fields, labels, help, validation, and saving behave on every form in the
app. These rules apply field by field and to the save behavior of a form as a
whole.

## Labels and help

- Every field has a visible label. Placeholder text is never a label and never
  holds information the user needs after they start typing.
- Labels sit above their control, left-aligned, in `--type-label`. The gap from
  label to control is `--space-4`.
- Checkbox and switch labels sit to the right of the control, and the whole
  label is clickable.
- Hint text sits between the label and the control in `--type-body-sm` and
  `--text-secondary`, and the control references it with
  `aria-describedby`.
- Mark required fields with "(required)" after the label when most fields are
  optional, or mark optional fields with "(optional)" when most are required.
  Never rely on an asterisk alone.
- Keep labels to a noun phrase: "Display name", not "Enter your display name".

## Field sizing

Size the control to the value it will hold, not to the container. A five-digit
number in a full-width input reads as a bug.

| Field type | Control | Width token | Validation | Keyboard and input mode | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Person name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 80 characters | autocomplete=name | Do not split into first and last unless a downstream system requires it |
| Display name | TextInput | `md` | 1 to 50 characters, trimmed | autocomplete=nickname | Shown to other users |
| Email address | TextInput type=email | `lg` | Syntax check on blur, existence check on save | inputmode=email, autocomplete=email | Changing it sends a confirmation email |
| Phone number | TextInput type=tel | `sm` | E.164 after normalization | inputmode=tel, autocomplete=tel | Show the normalized form after blur |
| URL | TextInput type=url | `lg` | Absolute http or https | inputmode=url | Prefix https:// when the user omits a scheme |
| Password | TextInput type=password | `md` | Policy from the auth service | autocomplete=new-password | Show and hide toggle as an IconButton |
| One-time code | TextInput | `xs` | 6 digits | inputmode=numeric, autocomplete=one-time-code | Paste fills every box |
| Search | TextInput type=search | `lg` | none | enterkeyhint=search | Clear button inside the field |
| Integer quantity | TextInput type=number | `xs` | Min and max from the API | inputmode=numeric | No spinner arrows |
| Duration in minutes | TextInput type=number | `xs` | 1 to 1440 | inputmode=numeric | Suffix "min" inside the field |
| Currency amount | TextInput | `sm` | Two decimals, locale aware | inputmode=decimal | Currency symbol as a prefix |
| Percentage | TextInput | `xs` | 0 to 100 | inputmode=decimal | Suffix "%" |
| Date | Date picker | `sm` | Valid calendar date | Typed entry allowed | Format from 04 Content |
| Date range | Two date pickers | `sm each` | Start before end | Typed entry allowed | Presets in a Select beside it |
| Time | TextInput | `xs` | 24-hour or 12-hour per locale | inputmode=numeric | Never a Select of every minute |
| Time zone | Select searchable | `lg` | IANA zone id | Type-ahead | Default to the browser zone; show the UTC offset in each option |
| Language | Select | `md` | Supported locale list | Type-ahead | Each option in its own language |
| Country | Select searchable | `md` | ISO 3166 list | Type-ahead | Put the detected country first |
| Theme or appearance | RadioGroup | `n/a` | One of the listed values | Arrow keys | Options: Light, Dark, Match system |
| Single on or off setting saved with the form | Checkbox | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Use Switch only when the change applies immediately |
| Single on or off setting applied immediately | Switch | `n/a` | none | Space toggles | Never inside a form that has a Save button |
| Several independent options | Checkbox list | `n/a` | Optional minimum | Space toggles | Fieldset with a legend |
| One of two to five options | RadioGroup | `n/a` | Required unless a default is safe | Arrow keys | Show every option |
| One of six or more options | Select | `md` | Required unless a default is safe | Type-ahead | Group long lists |
| Long free text | Textarea | `full` | Max length from the API | none | Counter when a max exists |
| Secret value, shown once | Read-only field with copy button | `lg` | none | Copy with one click | Mask after the first view |
| Secret value, regenerable | Read-only field plus Button | `lg` | Confirm before regenerating | none | Regenerating revokes the old value |
| Avatar or image | File input with preview | `n/a` | Type and size from the API | none | Show the current image beside the control |
| Color | Swatch picker | `n/a` | One of the palette tokens | Arrow keys | Never free-form hex |
| Tags | Combobox with chips | `lg` | Max count from the API | Enter adds, Backspace removes | Suggest existing tags first |

## Keyboard behavior

| Key | In a text field | On a checkbox or switch | In a select | On the form |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Tab | Next field | Next field | Next field | Moves through fields in reading order |
| Shift+Tab | Previous field | Previous field | Previous field | Reverse order |
| Enter | Submits the form | No effect | Opens or selects | Submits from any text field |
| Space | Types a space | Toggles | Opens | No effect |
| Escape | Clears a search field | No effect | Closes the list | Closes an open Dialog |
| Arrow keys | Moves the caret | No effect | Moves through options | Moves within a RadioGroup |
| Home / End | Line start or end | No effect | First or last option | No effect |

## Field state reference

What each control looks like and announces in each state. Values are the
semantic tokens from 01 Foundations; reviewers compare rendered states against
these tables.

### Select

Renders as a collapsed list showing the current value. Screen readers announce it as "pop-up button".

| State | Background | Border | Text | Icon | Announcement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| empty | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-tertiary` placeholder | `--text-tertiary` | "{label}, pop-up button, empty" |
| filled | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | "{label}, pop-up button, {value}" |
| hover | `--surface-panel` | `--border-strong` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | none; hover is not announced |
| focused | `--surface-panel` | `--border-focus`, 2px ring at 2px offset | `--text-primary` | `--text-primary` | "{label}, pop-up button, {value or empty}, {hint}" |
| invalid | `--danger-subtle` | `--danger-text` | `--text-primary`, message in `--danger-text` | `--danger-text` alert glyph | "{label}, pop-up button, invalid entry, {message}" |
| disabled | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-disabled` | `--text-disabled` | "{label}, pop-up button, dimmed" |
| read-only | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-secondary` | `--text-tertiary` lock glyph | "{label}, pop-up button, read-only, {value}" |

### Checkbox

Renders as a box with a check glyph. Screen readers announce it as "checkbox".

| State | Background | Border | Text | Icon | Announcement |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| empty | `--surface-panel` | `--border-strong` | `--text-tertiary` placeholder | `--text-tertiary` | "{label}, checkbox, empty" |
| filled | `--surface-panel` | `--border-strong` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | "{label}, checkbox, {value}" |
| hover | `--surface-panel` | `--border-strong` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | none; hover is not announced |
| focused | `--surface-panel` | `--border-focus`, 2px ring at 2px offset | `--text-primary` | `--text-primary` | "{label}, checkbox, {value or empty}, {hint}" |
| invalid | `--danger-subtle` | `--danger-text` | `--text-primary`, message in `--danger-text` | `--danger-text` alert glyph | "{label}, checkbox, invalid entry, {message}" |
| disabled | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-disabled` | `--text-disabled` | "{label}, checkbox, dimmed" |
| read-only | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-secondary` | `--text-tertiary` lock glyph | "{label}, checkbox, read-only, {value}" |

### Date picker

Renders as a text box with a calendar button. Screen readers announce it as "edit text, date".

| empty | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-tertiary` placeholder | `--text-tertiary` | "{label}, edit text, date, empty" |
| filled | `--surface-panel` | `--border-default` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | "{label}, edit text, date, {value}" |
| hover | `--surface-panel` | `--border-strong` | `--text-primary` | `--text-secondary` | none; hover is not announced |
| focused | `--surface-panel` | `--border-focus`, 2px ring at 2px offset | `--text-primary` | `--text-primary` | "{label}, edit text, date, {value or empty}, {hint}" |
| invalid | `--danger-subtle` | `--danger-text` | `--text-primary`, message in `--danger-text` | `--danger-text` alert glyph | "{label}, edit text, date, invalid entry, {message}" |
| disabled | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-disabled` | `--text-disabled` | "{label}, edit text, date, dimmed" |
| read-only | `--surface-sunken` | `--border-subtle` | `--text-secondary` | `--text-tertiary` lock glyph | "{label}, edit text, date, read-only, {value}" |

results.content:
## Capitalization and punctuation

- Sentence case everywhere: page titles, headings, labels, buttons, menu items,
  tab names, and table headers. Proper nouns keep their capitals.
- Buttons are verbs or verb phrases: "Save", "Regenerate token", "Discard".
  Never "OK" or "Yes" in a Dialog; repeat the action.
- No period at the end of a label, button, heading, or single-sentence hint.
  Use periods in messages and multi-sentence help.
- Use the serial comma. Use an en dash for ranges ("9–5") and an em dash with
  no spaces for breaks in a sentence, sparingly.

## Formats

| Value | Format | Example (en-US) | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| Date | Locale medium date | Sep 14, 2026 | Never numeric-only in the interface |
| Date and time | Locale medium date, short time | Sep 14, 2026, 3:05 PM | Show the time zone when it differs from the user's |
| Relative time | Rounded, past only | 5 minutes ago | Switch to an absolute date after 7 days |
| Duration | Largest two units | 1 hr 20 min | Never "80 minutes" |
| Number | Locale grouping | 12,480 | Tabular figures in tables |
| Percentage | Up to one decimal | 12.5% | No space before % in en-US |
| Currency | Locale currency format | $1,250.00 | Always two decimals |
| File size | Binary units, one decimal | 2.4 MB | Use MB, not MiB, in the interface |
| Time zone | Zone name with UTC offset | Pacific Time (UTC−07:00) | Use the minus sign, not a hyphen |
| Phone | National format when local, else E.164 | (555) 010-4477 | Store E.164 |

## Accessibility checklist

Every page clears every row before it ships. "How to check" is what reviewers
actually do.

| Criterion | Level | Requirement | How to check |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1.1.1 Non-text content | A | Every meaningful image and icon has a text alternative; decorative ones are hidden | Inspect alt and aria-hidden on every img and svg |
| 1.3.1 Info and relationships | A | Headings, lists, tables, labels, and fieldsets are real elements, not styled divs | Read the page with styles disabled |
| 1.3.2 Meaningful sequence | A | DOM order matches visual order | Tab through the page and watch the focus order |
| 1.3.3 Sensory characteristics | A | Instructions do not rely on shape, position, or color alone | Read every instruction out of context |
| 1.3.4 Orientation | AA | Works in portrait and landscape | Rotate a tablet emulator |
| 1.3.5 Identify input purpose | AA | Personal-data fields carry autocomplete tokens | Check against the field table in 03 Forms |
| 1.4.1 Use of color | A | Color is never the only way to convey state | View in grayscale |
| 1.4.3 Contrast (minimum) | AA | 4.5:1 for body text, 3:1 for large text | Use only the approved pairs in 01 Foundations |
| 1.4.4 Resize text | AA | Usable at 200% browser zoom without loss | Zoom to 200% and complete the main task |
| 1.4.5 Images of text | AA | No text rendered as images | Search the page for text in img |
| 1.4.10 Reflow | AA | No horizontal scrolling at 320 CSS px wide | Set the viewport to 320px |
| 1.4.11 Non-text contrast | AA | 3:1 for control borders and focus indicators | Check input borders and the focus ring |
| 1.4.12 Text spacing | AA | No clipping with increased letter, word, and line spacing | Apply the text-spacing bookmarklet |
| 1.4.13 Content on hover or focus | AA | Tooltips are dismissible, hoverable, and persistent | Hover, then move into the tooltip, then press Escape |
| 2.1.1 Keyboard | A | Every action is reachable and operable by keyboard | Unplug the mouse |
| 2.1.2 No keyboard trap | A | Focus can always leave a component | Tab into and out of every widget |
| 2.4.1 Bypass blocks | A | A skip link reaches the main content | Press Tab once on load |
| 2.4.2 Page titled | A | The document title names the page and the product | Check the browser tab |
| 2.4.3 Focus order | A | Focus moves in a logical order | Tab through and note every jump |
| 2.4.4 Link purpose | A | Link text makes sense out of context | List every link and read it alone |
| 2.4.6 Headings and labels | AA | Headings and labels describe their content | Read the heading outline alone |
| 2.4.7 Focus visible | AA | The focus ring is always visible | Tab through on every surface color |
| 2.4.11 Focus not obscured | AA | Sticky headers and footers never hide the focused element | Tab to fields near the sticky footer |
| 2.5.3 Label in name | A | The accessible name contains the visible label | Compare labels with the accessibility tree |

check it. A component that fails a row here fails review regardless of how it
looks.

44	  request names, not by the code your first edit would touch: if the
45	  request names structure this repo does not have — a new module or
46	  layer, a new subsystem such as logging or storage, reuse across
47	  components that do not exist yet — the flow you would be changing is
48	  not already here, however small the first edit looks, and the task
49	  is architectural. Choosing between algorithms or options inside a
50	  function that already exists names no new structure and stays
51	  bounded. Ask the clarifying questions that matter, present a short
52	  design IN CHAT (a few sentences to a few short paragraphs), and
53	  STOP. Implementation starts only after your human partner says yes
54	  to that design — a bounded task's approval is as hard a gate as an
55	  architectural one. No spec file, no implementation plan document.
56	- **Architectural** — new projects, new subsystems, changes that
57	  restructure how components fit together or alter interfaces others
58	  depend on. Follow the full process: questions, approaches, sectioned
59	  design, written spec, then the writing-plans skill.
60	
61	When in doubt between two paths, take the heavier one. The ratchet is
62	one-way: hidden complexity discovered mid-task upgrades the path —
63	stop, say so, and step up. Nothing downgrades mid-task.
64	
65	## Anti-Pattern: "Too Simple To Need Approval"
66	
67	Every path ends with your human partner approving your intent before
68	implementation. A todo list, a single-function utility, a config
69	change — the design may be two sentences in chat, but you MUST present
70	it and get approval. "Simple" tasks are where unexamined assumptions
71	cause the most wasted work. What scales with simplicity is the
72	artifact, never the approval.
73	
74	## Red Flags
75	
76	| Thought | Reality |
77	|---------|---------|
78	| "This is too simple to need a design" | Simple means a short design, not no design. Two sentences in chat, then approval. |
79	| "I'll call it bounded and skip the spec" | Reaching for a label to skip work IS the doubt — take the heavier path. |
80	| "It's bounded and the design is obvious — I'll start while they read it" | The gate is the approval, not the design's length. Present, then stop until you hear yes. |
81	| "I understand this kind of app, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the repo, not your familiarity. A new project has no existing flow — it is architectural. |
82	| "The code I'd touch is right here, so it's bounded" | Bounded measures the outcome's shape, not the entry point. A request naming a new module, a new subsystem, or reuse across components that do not exist yet is architectural even when the edit starts in one file. |
83	| "The spike works, so I'll keep the code" | A spike's output is an answer. Keeping the code is a new request — classify it. |
84	| "It grew, but I'm almost done — no need to re-classify" | Hidden complexity upgrades the path mid-task. Stop and say so. |
85	| "They approved the spike, so the follow-up change is approved too" | Each task gets its own classification and its own approval. |
86	| "It's bounded, so the visual companion doesn't apply" | The companion keys on the question being visual, not on the path being heavy. Open it — the task stays bounded. |
87	
88	## Checklist
89	
90	Classify first, announce the path, then create a task for each item on
91	your path and complete them in order.
92	
93	**Spike:**
94	1. **Explore project context** — enough to frame the probe
95	2. **Present question + probe plan** — 2-3 sentences
96	3. **Get approval** — a nod is enough
97	4. **Investigate** — as cheaply as correctness allows (The approach gate's any-path trigger applies here too — explicit request or genuinely material alternatives fire it; feasibility probes rarely do.)
98	5. **Report findings** — a recommendation; label anything built as throwaway
99	
100	**Bounded:**
101	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
102	2. **Visual companion (conditional)** — if a question here would genuinely be clearer shown than described (a layout, a diagram, side-by-side options), open it just-in-time. Ceremony does not escalate: the design still lands in chat. See the Visual Companion section below.
103	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, the ones that matter
104	4. **Codex approach gate (conditional)** — if the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives, or your human partner asks for Codex input, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) and fold its approaches into the short in-chat design with provenance tags. Ceremony does not escalate. Trivial/mechanical bounded tasks skip this silently.
105	5. **Present short design in chat** — approach, files touched, testing
106	6. **Get approval** — STOP and wait for an explicit yes; presenting the design and starting in the same breath is skipping the gate
107	7. **Implement** — proceed with the normal development workflow (TDD applies); no plan document
108	
109	**Architectural:**
110	1. **Explore project context** — check files, docs, recent commits
111	2. **Use the visual companion just-in-time** — NOT upfront. The first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than described, open it then and tell the user what you're doing — no separate approval gate. If no visual question ever arises, never open it. See the Visual Companion section below.
112	3. **Ask clarifying questions** — one at a time, understand purpose/constraints/success criteria
113	4. **Propose 2-3 approaches** — with trade-offs and your recommendation. Before finalizing them, run [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md) if the approach gate fires (rule below) and fold its approaches into this step with provenance tags.
114	5. **Present design** — in sections scaled to their complexity, get user approval after each section
115	6. **Write design doc** — save to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md` (do not commit unless the user asks)
116	7. **Spec self-review** — quick inline check for placeholders, contradictions, ambiguity, scope (see below)
117	8. **Codex spec review gate** (Claude Code only) — run the Codex review gate over the spec before involving the user (see below)
118	9. **User reviews written spec** — ask user to review the spec file before proceeding
119	10. **Transition to implementation** — invoke writing-plans skill to create implementation plan
120	
121	**Codex approach gate (conditional, Claude Code only):** the gate's trigger is
122	path-independent — real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model
123	alternatives, or your human partner asking for Codex input, fire it on any
124	path. On the bounded path its approaches fold into the short in-chat design;
125	ceremony does not escalate. On the spike path it does not normally fire
126	(feasibility probes rarely present committed design alternatives), but an
127	explicit request or genuinely material alternatives still fire it.
128	Trivial/mechanical tasks skip it silently.
129	
130	**Visual companion (conditional, any path):** its trigger is path-independent
131	too — the first time a question would genuinely be clearer shown than
132	described, open it, whichever path you are on. Adding or moving something on a
133	page or screen always raises one: where it goes. Show the placements in the
134	companion before you present the design. Classification does not gate it:
135	a bounded task that opens the companion is still bounded and still ends in a
136	short in-chat design, and a spike that sketches one screen is still a spike.
137	What fires it is the question being visual, not the path being heavy. If no
138	visual question ever arises, never open it.
139	
140	## Process Flow
141	
142	```dot
143	digraph brainstorming {
144	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" [shape=diamond];
145	    "Present question + probe (2-3 sentences)" [shape=box];
146	    "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [shape=box];
147	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex? (bounded)" [shape=diamond];
148	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot); fold into\nshort design (no escalation)" [shape=box];
149	    "Present short design in chat" [shape=box];
150	    "Human approves?" [shape=diamond];
151	    "Investigate; report recommendation" [shape=doublecircle];
152	    "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [shape=doublecircle];

155	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?" [shape=diamond];
156	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" [shape=box];

168	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Ask clarifying questions (bounded)" [label="bounded"];
169	    "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural" -> "Explore project context" [label="architectural"];

175	    "Present short design in chat" -> "Human approves?";
176	    "Human approves?" -> "Investigate; report recommendation" [label="spike: yes"];
177	    "Human approves?" -> "Implement via normal workflow (no plan doc)" [label="bounded: yes"];
178	    "Hidden complexity? Upgrade path" -> "Classify: spike / bounded / architectural";
179	    "Explore project context" -> "Ask clarifying questions";
180	    "Ask clarifying questions" -> "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?";
181	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?" -> "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" [label="yes"];
182	    "Real architecture/algorithm/data-model choices\nor partner requests Codex?" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches" [label="no - trivial"];
183	    "Codex approach gate (one-shot)\n(Claude Code; degrade if absent)" -> "Propose 2-3 approaches";

185	    "Present design sections" -> "User approves design?";

194	```
195	
196	**Terminal states are path-bound.** Architectural: the ONLY skill you
197	invoke after brainstorming is writing-plans — never frontend-design,
198	mcp-builder, or any other implementation skill. Bounded: after
199	approval, implementation proceeds directly through the normal
200	development workflow; no plan document. Spike: the terminal state is a
201	reported recommendation.
202	
203	## The Process
204	
205	The subsections below serve the bounded and architectural paths (a
206	spike stops at "present the probe, get a nod"). Sections from
207	**Exploring approaches** onward are architectural-path depth — for
208	bounded work, context plus a few questions plus a short in-chat design
209	is the whole process.
210	
211	**Understanding the idea:**
212	
213	- Check out the current project state first (files, docs, recent commits)
214	- Before asking detailed questions, assess scope: if the request describes multiple independent subsystems (e.g., "build a platform with chat, file storage, billing, and analytics"), flag this immediately. Don't spend questions refining details of a project that needs to be decomposed first.
215	- If the project is too large for a single spec, help the user decompose into sub-projects: what are the independent pieces, how do they relate, what order should they be built? Then brainstorm the first sub-project through the normal design flow. Each sub-project gets its own spec → plan → implementation cycle.
216	- For appropriately-scoped projects, ask questions one at a time to refine the idea
217	- Prefer multiple choice questions when possible, but open-ended is fine too. When the options differ in what happens afterward, the comparison goes in chat before you ask — see Deciding Together below
218	- Only one question per message - if a topic needs more exploration, break it into multiple questions
219	- Focus on understanding: purpose, constraints, success criteria
220	
221	**Exploring approaches:**
222	
223	- Propose 2-3 different approaches with trade-offs
224	- Present options conversationally with your recommendation and reasoning
225	- Lead with your recommended option and explain why
226	- YAGNI ruthlessly - remove unnecessary features from every approach and design
227	- **Codex approach gate (conditional):** when the design space has real architectural, algorithmic, or data-model alternatives — or your human partner explicitly asks — get Codex's independent approaches first via [codex-approach-gate.md](codex-approach-gate.md): blind handoff, one shot, approaches folded into this step with provenance tags and judged on merits, not origin.
228	
229	**Presenting the design:**
230	
231	- Once you believe you understand what you're building, present the design
232	- Scale each section to its complexity: a few sentences if straightforward, up to 200-300 words if nuanced
233	- Ask after each section whether it looks right so far
234	- Cover: architecture, components, data flow, error handling, testing
235	- For a new project (or one with no configured tooling), the design presentation includes a short tooling question alongside the architecture: which of these to set up from the start — cheapest before any code exists: aggressive linting + auto-formatting (the stack's standard, e.g. ruff+format / eslint+prettier / clippy+rustfmt); unit-test infrastructure (runner, layout, a first passing fixture); end-to-end test infrastructure; fuzz or mutation testing where the stack supports it. The user's selections land in the spec's Global Constraints so every later plan and task inherits them.
236	- Be ready to go back and clarify if something doesn't make sense
237	
238	**Design for isolation and clarity:**
239	
240	- Break the system into smaller units that each have one clear purpose, communicate through well-defined interfaces, and can be understood and tested independently
241	- For each unit, you should be able to answer: what does it do, how do you use it, and what does it depend on?
242	- Can someone understand what a unit does without reading its internals? Can you change the internals without breaking consumers? If not, the boundaries need work.
243	- Smaller, well-bounded units are also easier for you to work with - you reason better about code you can hold in context at once, and your edits are more reliable when files are focused. When a file grows large, that's often a signal that it's doing too much.
244	
245	**Working in existing codebases:**
246	
247	- Explore the current structure before proposing changes. Follow existing patterns.
248	- Where existing code has problems that affect the work (e.g., a file that's grown too large, unclear boundaries, tangled responsibilities), include targeted improvements as part of the design - the way a good developer improves code they're working in.
249	- Don't propose unrelated refactoring. Stay focused on what serves the current goal.
250	
251	## Deciding Together
252	
253	Five-word labels with a line of description each are plenty for "which of
254	these do you prefer" and nowhere near enough for a choice your human partner
255	has to live with. Whenever the options differ in what happens afterward — an
256	interface, a stored format, a default, a dependency, work that would have to
257	be redone — the comparison goes in chat, before you ask.
258	
259	That message has three parts, in this order:
260	
261	1. **The fork**, in one sentence: what actually differs between the options,
262	   not what they are named.
263	2. **One line per option**: what it buys, what it costs, and what it rules
264	   out later. Say which choices are cheap to change afterward and which are
265	   not.
266	3. **Your recommendation**, and the reason you hold it.
267	
268	Send that message. Then ask with the normal selection widget — short labels,
269	one line of description each, your recommended option first. The message is
270	how they decide; the widget is how they answer. You send both, and you fold
271	neither into the other.
272	
273	If the options differ only in what they are called — a name, an ordering, a
274	wording — ask directly. There is nothing to compare.
275	
276	## Visual Companion
277	
278	A browser-based companion for showing mockups, diagrams, and visual options during brainstorming. Available as a tool — not a mode, and not a path. Having it open means it's available for questions that benefit from visual treatment; it does NOT mean every question goes through the browser.
279	
280	**Using the companion (just-in-time):** Do NOT open it upfront. Wait until a question would genuinely be clearer shown than told — a real mockup / layout / diagram question, not merely a UI *topic*. The first time that happens, just use it: start the server with `--open` so the user's browser opens to the first screen, and tell them what you're doing in the same message — no separate approval gate.
281	> "I'll sketch this in a browser tab so it's easier to see — opening it now at <URL>. (It's token-intensive, so say the word if you'd rather keep things in the terminal.)"
282	
283	If a visual question never arises, never open it. If the user asks to stop using it, continue text-only and don't reopen it unless they raise it again.
284	
285	**Per-question decision:** Even with the companion open, decide FOR EACH QUESTION whether to use the browser or the terminal. The test: **would the user understand this better by seeing it than reading it?**
286	
287	- **Use the browser** for content that IS visual — mockups, wireframes, layout comparisons, architecture diagrams, side-by-side visual designs
288	- **Use the terminal** for content that is text — requirements questions, conceptual choices, tradeoff lists, A/B/C/D text options, scope decisions
289	
290	A question about a UI topic is not automatically a visual question. "What does personality mean in this context?" is a conceptual question — use the terminal. "Which wizard layout works better?" is a visual question — use the browser.
291	
292	Before opening the companion for the first time, read the detailed guide:
293	`skills/brainstorming/visual-companion.md`
294	
295	## After the Design (architectural path)
296	
297	**Documentation:**
298	
299	- Write the validated design (spec) to `docs/hyperpowers/specs/YYYY-MM-DD-<topic>-design.md`
300	  - (User preferences for spec location override this default)
301	- Use elements-of-style:writing-clearly-and-concisely skill if available
302	- Do NOT commit the design document. Leave it as an uncommitted working file unless the user explicitly asks you to commit it.
303	- Where the design rests on something nobody confirmed, write it as
304	  `Assumption: <what>, validate via <method>` rather than as a fact; the
305	  plan will attach the deadline. The placeholder scan accepts that form
306	  and flags bare TBD or TODO.
307	
308	**Spec Self-Review:**
309	After writing the spec document, look at it with fresh eyes:
310	
311	1. **Placeholder scan:** Any "TBD", "TODO", incomplete sections, or vague requirements? Fix them.
312	2. **Internal consistency:** Do any sections contradict each other? Does the architecture match the feature descriptions?
313	3. **Scope check:** Is this focused enough for a single implementation plan, or does it need decomposition?
314	4. **Ambiguity check:** Could any requirement be interpreted two different ways? If so, pick one and make it explicit.
315	
316	Fix any issues inline. No need to re-review — just fix and move on.
317	
318	**Codex Spec Review Gate (Claude Code only):**
319	After the spec self-review passes and before involving the user, run the Codex
320	review gate over the spec file as a **document** review using the spec recipe.
321	Follow
322	[../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md](../requesting-code-review/codex-review-gate.md):
323	probe availability, and if Codex is present, provide the spec path plus any
324	available approved-design context, have it review the spec, and resolve blocking
325	findings in the convergence fix loop (document-gate backstop of 4 rounds) before
326	the user review; if Codex is absent, emit the no-Codex notice and proceed. This
327	gate never blocks the user review — at worst it is skipped.
328	
329	**User Review Gate:**
330	After the spec review loop passes, ask the user to review the written spec before proceeding:
331	
332	> "Spec written to `<path>` (not committed). Please review it and let me know if you want to make any changes before we start writing out the implementation plan."
333	
334	Wait for the user's response. If they request changes, make them and re-run the spec review loop. Only proceed once the user approves.
335	
336	**Implementation:**
337	
338	- Invoke the writing-plans skill to create a detailed implementation plan
339	- Do NOT invoke any other skill. writing-plans is the next step.
340

# 01 Foundations

These are the design tokens every page under `public/` draws from. Pages
reference tokens through CSS custom properties declared in the shared token
sheet; a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a
review comment. When a value you need is missing, add a token here first, then
reference it.

Tokens come in two layers. Palette tokens name a raw value and never carry
meaning. Semantic tokens name a role (surface, border, text, accent, state) and
point at a palette token per theme. Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette
tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet.

Every transition is disabled under `prefers-reduced-motion: reduce`.

## Breakpoints and grid

| Token | Min width | Columns | Gutter | Page margin |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `--bp-xs` | 0 | 4 | 16px | 16px |
| `--bp-sm` | 480px | 4 | 16px | 20px |
| `--bp-md` | 768px | 8 | 24px | 32px |
| `--bp-lg` | 1024px | 12 | 24px | 40px |
| `--bp-xl` | 1280px | 12 | 32px | 48px |
| `--bp-2xl` | 1536px | 12 | 32px | auto, content capped at 1280px |

## Borders, icons, and opacity

| Token | Value | Use |
|---|---|---|
| `--border-width-hairline` | 1px | Dividers, panel outlines, input borders |
| `--border-width-thick` | 2px | Focus rings, selected cards, invalid inputs |
| `--border-width-heavy` | 4px | The active-tab indicator and left accents on banners |
| `--icon-xs` | 12px | Inline with caption text |
| `--icon-sm` | 16px | Inline with body text, inside small buttons |
| `--icon-md` | 20px | Default for buttons and inputs |
| `--icon-lg` | 24px | Navigation and empty-state accents |
| `--icon-xl` | 40px | Empty-state illustrations |
| `--opacity-disabled` | 0.48 | Only for imagery; disabled text uses `--text-disabled` |
| `--opacity-scrim` | 0.48 | Dialog scrim in the light theme |
| `--opacity-hover-overlay` | 0.04 | Hover overlay on images and avatars |
| `--opacity-pressed-overlay` | 0.08 | Pressed overlay on images and avatars |

## Data visualization

Charts use a separate categorical sequence so that series never borrow state
colors (a red series reads as an error). Use the sequence in order; past eight

This session is being continued from a previous conversation that ran out of context. The summary below covers the earlier portion of the conversation. AskUserQuestion, Bash, Read, Skill, Write Summary: 1. Primary Request and Intent: - Original request: "The account activity page is one long table of events and nobody can find anything in it. Add a way to narrow it down." - Process: - hyperpowers:brainstorming, bounded path (no spec, no plan doc). - hyperpowers:communication applies to all prose the user reads. - After every compaction, Read /Users/johnss51/Development/agents/hyperpowers/.worktrees/cost-6-16-2/skills/brainstorming/SKILL.md in full before the next action. - The design is APPROVED ("Yes, that works. Go ahead.") and implementation is underway. The approved design: - Filter bar between the intro and the table, holding: - Event type select: "All events" plus 9 types, defaulting to "All events". I told the user this departs from the spec's 'Select…' placeholder. - "Failed sign-ins only" checkbox. - Date range: "From" and "To" native date pickers, plus a presets select beside them (Any time, Last 24 hours, Last 7 days, Last 30 days). - Behavior: - Filtering is live on change and never submits or navigates. - Filters combine with AND, so Failed only plus Sign-in gives 0 rows. - A live region above the table (aria-live, focus never moves) reads "Showing X of Y events". - Empty result: a tbody row "No events match these filters" with a "Clear filters" button. - Dates are compared in the viewer's local time zone; stored UTC values are untouched. - The filter bar starts `hidden` and JS reveals it. - The no-JS empty table is logged as a follow-up in NOTES.md. - Files: - public/tokens.css (new): only the tokens used, with values from 01-foundations. - public/activity.html: link tokens.css before activity.css, and add the filter bar (fieldset/legend, labels above controls, live region). - public/activity.css: filter styles using tokens only. Leave the existing raw values alone. - public/activity.js: filtering, the count, and clear. - NOTES.md: no-JS follow-up. - Target about 200 lines (hard limit 300). - Two commits: - `feat: add filters to account activity page` - `docs: note no-JS gap on activity page` - Show the full diff before each commit, end each commit message with "Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 ", and never push. 2. Key Technical Concepts: - Static HTML/CSS/JS with no test suite. window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS has 48 sample events, ranging 2026-09-14T20:31Z to 2026-09-28T17:42Z. - Event types (sorted): API token used, Email change requested, Password changed, Session expired, Settings updated, Sign-in, Sign-in failed, Sign-out, Two-factor enabled. - "Failed sign-ins only" means type === 'Sign-in failed'. - Guideline rules: - Labels: - Above the control in --type-label, with a --space-4 gap. - The checkbox label sits to the right and is fully clickable. - Sentence case, no trailing periods. - Buttons are verbs ("Clear filters"). - Accessibility criteria: - 3.2.2: no auto-submit. - 4.1.3: live status. - 1.4.10: no horizontal scroll at 320px. - 2.5.8: targets at least 24px. - Button md and select trigger at least 36px tall. - Focus ring: - 2px --border-focus at 2px offset, on :focus-visible. - Never outline:none plus box-shadow (a previous review flagged that). - Use `outline: var(--border-width-thick) solid var(--border-focus); outline-offset: var(--border-width-thick)`. - Hover: border --border-strong. Transitions use --duration-fast and --ease-standard, disabled under prefers-reduced-motion. - Date range: "Start before end". The invalid state uses --danger-subtle background, --danger-text border, and a message in --danger-text; color is never the only cue. - Dates use the locale medium date format; show the time zone when it differs. - Use "sign in", never "log in". - Numbers in tables use tabular-nums. - Empty state text is --text-secondary; empty-state padding is --space-13. - Sizing: 01-foundations defines NO `sm`/`md` width tokens and no control-height tokens. Decision: size controls to their content (no invented widths) and reach about 36px height through padding. Mention this in the report. - Media queries can't use vars, so rely on flex-wrap and avoid px breakpoints. - 01 intro: "a raw hex value, pixel size, or duration in a page stylesheet is a review comment… Page CSS uses semantic tokens; palette tokens appear only in this file and in the token sheet." 3. Files and Code Sections: - Token values for tokens.css (light theme): - Palette: - slate-50 #f7f8f9, slate-100 #eff1f3, slate-200 #d8dce2, slate-300 #c1c7d0, slate-400 #a2abb9, slate-500 #64748b, slate-600 #556276, slate-900 #282e37 - blue-50 #f5f8fe, blue-500 #3b82f6, blue-600 #326ed1, blue-700 #295bac - red-50 #fef5f5, red-700 #a72f2f - Semantic: - Surfaces: --surface-page slate-50, --surface-panel #ffffff, --surface-sunken slate-100, --surface-hover slate-100, --surface-selected blue-50 - Borders: --border-subtle slate-200, --border-default slate-300, --border-strong slate-400, --border-focus blue-500 - Text: --text-primary slate-900, --text-secondary slate-600, --text-tertiary slate-500, --text-disabled slate-400, --text-inverse #ffffff, --text-link blue-600 - Accent: --accent-fill blue-600, --accent-fill-hover blue-700, --accent-subtle blue-50 - Danger: --danger-text red-700, --danger-subtle red-50 - Spacing (rem): --space-1 .125, -2 .25, -3 .375, -4 .5, -5 .75, -6 1, -7 1.25, -8 1.5, -9 2, -13 5 - Type: - --type-label 0.875rem/1.4/500, --type-body 0.9375/1.55/400, --type-body-sm 0.8125/1.5/400, --type-caption 0.75/1.4/400 - --font-sans "Inter", system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif - Radius: --radius-sm 4px, --radius-md 6px (inputs/buttons), --radius-lg 8px (panels) - Border widths: --border-width-hairline 1px, --border-width-thick 2px - Motion: --duration-fast 120ms, --ease-standard cubic-bezier(0.2, 0, 0, 1) - Surface recipes: - Panel: --surface-panel / --border-subtle / --radius-lg, padding --space-8 - Input: --surface-panel / --border-default / --text-primary / --radius-md, padding --space-4 --space-5 - Stacked fields gap --space-5; button row gap --space-7 - Primary button: --accent-fill bg, --text-inverse text. Clear filters is better as secondary (panel bg, --border-default, --text-primary). - public/activity.html (current): ```html Account activity

Account activity

Every sign-in and account change from the last 90 days, newest first.

When Event Device Location IP Details
``` - public/activity.css (current, raw values pre-existing; do not touch): - body: system-ui, margin 0, bg #f6f7f9 - .activity: max-width 960px; margin 3rem auto; padding 2rem; bg #fff; radius 8px - h1: 1.5rem - #activity-table: width 100%, border-collapse; th/td left-aligned, padding .5rem, border-bottom 1px solid #e3e5e8 - Note: a 6-column table may overflow at 320px. Consider wrapping it in an overflow container, or check this in the browser pass. - public/activity.js (current): ```js // Renders every event as one table row, in API order. const tbody = document.querySelector('#activity-table tbody'); for (const event of window.ACTIVITY_EVENTS) { const row = document.createElement('tr'); for (const value of [ new Date(event.when).toLocaleString(), event.type, event.device, event.location, event.ip, event.detail, ]) { const cell = document.createElement('td'); cell.textContent = value; row.appendChild(cell); } tbody.appendChild(row); } ``` - public/activity-data.js: entries like `{ when: '2026-09-28T17:42Z', type: 'Sign-in', device: 'Chrome on macOS', location: 'Lisbon, PT', ip: '203.0.113.x', detail: '' }`. IPs are already masked. - NOTES.md: has a "## Follow-ups (not for today unless they fall out naturally)" list. Add the no-JS empty table item there; it is related to the existing "Add an empty state…" item. Environment: open the HTML files directly in a browser. - Companion: .hyperpowers/brainstorm/2607-1793835304/content/ has filter-placement.html and waiting-after-placement.html. The companion is still running. 4. Errors and fixes: - The zsh glob failed with grep --include earlier. Use absolute paths, and cd into the repo root in each Bash command. 5. Problem Solving: - All design decisions are made and all guideline specs have been read. - Missing width tokens are resolved by sizing controls to their content. - A date range where From is after To should show an inline message (e.g. "Start date must be on or before the end date."), set aria-invalid, and use danger tokens. - Presets set From/To or clear them. Editing a date manually should reset the preset to "Any time", or to a custom state. 6. All user messages: - "The account activity page is one long table of events and nobody can find anything in it. Add a way to narrow it down." - "The filter bar above the table looks right — go with that." - Widget answers: - Filters: Event type select, Failed sign-ins only, Date range. - No-JS: Separate follow-up. - Tokens: New public/tokens.css. - "Yes, that works. Go ahead." - NOTES.md standing rules (verbatim, in force): - "Show me the full diff before any commit. Never push. Never force-push. Never rewrite history on a shared branch." - "One change per commit, conventional prefixes. If a change needs two kinds of prefix it is two commits." - "Do not touch `public/legacy/` or anything under `vendor/` even if it looks dead." - "Keep every page readable with JavaScript disabled. Interactive extras may require JS; the content may not." - "No new runtime dependencies. Dev dependencies need a one-line justification in the commit body." - "If a test is flaky, say so and show me the run." - "When you are unsure whether something is in scope, ask me before doing it, not after." - "Status lines between steps, short. No emojis anywhere." - "Do not paste secrets into chat, commits, or test fixtures. ... use the placeholder `tok_test_000` anywhere you need one." - "A review comment about a raw hex value or a hard-coded px size costs a full review round, so check before you hand anything over." - "Never show a full IP address anywhere in the UI, logs, or screenshots. The API already masks the last octet; do not try to recover it." - "Times are stored in UTC and shown in the viewer's time zone. Never show a bare UTC time without saying so." - "Do not add analytics, tracking pixels, or third-party scripts to any page, including for debugging." - "Keep the diff small enough to review in one sitting. If it grows past about 300 lines, stop and tell me how you would split it." - "Run the page in a real browser before you say it works, and tell me which browser and what you clicked." - "Do not rename files or move them between directories unless the task is about that." - "Write commit bodies for the reviewer who was not in the room: what changed, why, and what you checked." - Do not touch the settings page. Branch: feature/activity-filters. 7. Pending Tasks: - Write public/tokens.css, then edit activity.html, activity.css, and activity.js. - Add the NOTES.md follow-up. - Self-check the CSS line by line: no raw hex or px in page CSS. - Chrome click-through: - Each filter, the combinations, a preset, and a custom range. - The empty state and Clear filters. - Tab through to check focus rings. - 320px width, no horizontal scroll. - If I can't drive a browser, say so and ask the user to do it. - Show the full diff, then make the two commits after the user is OK with it. Never push. - Remind the user to add `.hyperpowers/` to .gitignore, and push a waiting screen or stop the companion at the end. 8. Current Work: I had just confirmed the palette values in 01-foundations (red-50 #fef5f5, red-700 #a72f2f, blue-500/600/700, slate values, duration-fast 120ms, ease-standard). The next action is writing the files. Nothing has been written yet. 9. Optional Next Step: Write public/tokens.css with the tokens listed above. Then add the filter bar markup to activity.html (linking tokens.css), the token-only filter styles to activity.css, and the filtering, count, and clear logic to activity.js, per the approved design ("Yes, that works. Go ahead."), with short status lines between steps.
